es.summary: Acumulación excesiva de líquido en el tejido cerebral que aumenta la presión intracraneal y compromete la función neurológica.
key_points: Aumento de la presión intracraneal (PIC) > 20 mmHg es crítico.
Causas comunes: trauma, tumor, infección, insuficiencia cardíaca y desequilibrios de proteínas plasmáticas.
Síntomas incluyen cefalea, vómitos, alteración del nivel de conciencia y papiledema.
Diagnóstico se basa en TC o RMN y medición de PIC mediante monitor invasivo.
Tratamiento: manejo de la causa, diuréticos osmóticos y control de la PIC.

pathophysiology: Daño o inflamación cerebral altera la barrera hematoencefálica.
Se incrementa la permeabilidad capilar y se retiene líquido intersticial.
El volumen intracraneal aumenta, elevando la presión intracraneal.
La perfusión cerebral disminuye por compresión de vasos arteriales.
signs_symptoms: Cefalea intensa que empeora al acostarse.
Vómitos sin náuseas o con contenido alimenticio.
Alteración del nivel de conciencia (confusión, somnolencia).
Pupilas desiguales o reacción lenta a la luz.
Papiledema al examen de fondo de ojo.
diagnostics: Tomografía computarizada (TC) de cráneo: hipodensidad difusa.
Resonancia magnética (RMN): edema vasogénico o citotóxico.
Monitor invasivo de PIC: valores >20 mmHg indican hipertensión intracraneal.
Laboratorio: glucosa 70‑100 mg/dL, electrolitos Na⁺ 135‑145 mEq/L, K⁺ 3.5‑5.0 mEq/L.
treatment: Elevación de la cabecera 30°‑45° para favorecer drenaje venoso.
Diuréticos osmóticos (manitol) para reducir la PIC.
Control de la causa subyacente (antibióticos, cirugía, control de insuficiencia cardíaca).
Ventilación mecánica con presión positiva al final de la espiración (PEEP) si hay compromiso respiratorio.
complications: Herniación cerebral con compromiso de la tronco encefálico.
Isquemia cerebral por disminución del flujo sanguíneo.
nursing_care: Monitorear signos vitales y presión arterial cada hora.
Evaluar nivel de conciencia usando la escala de Glasgow.
Mantener la cabeza elevada y evitar maniobras que aumenten la PIC.
Registrar salida de orina y balance hídrico.
Administrar diuréticos osmóticos según indicación médica.
patient_teaching: Explicar la importancia de mantener la cabeza elevada.
Enseñar a reconocer signos de empeoramiento (cefalea intensa, vómitos).
Instruir sobre la necesidad de cumplir con el tratamiento y controles de imagen.
Promover evitar esfuerzos que aumenten la presión intratorácica (toser, maniobras de Valsalva).

evidenced_by: disminución de la tolerancia al esfuerzo
cambios en la escala de Glasgow con actividad
outcomes: Tolerancia a la actividad aumentada a 30 min sin signos de fatiga (Escala de Borg <3)
Nivel de fatiga ≤3 en escala de 0‑10 dentro de 48 h

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de conciencia y escala de Glasgow cada 2 h
interventions.rationale: Detectar deterioro neurológico temprano.

interventions.action: Monitorear signos vitales y presión arterial cada hora
interventions.rationale: Identificar cambios hemodinámicos que puedan empeorar la PIC.

interventions.action: Mantener la cabecera de la cama en posición semi-Fowler (30°‑45°)
interventions.rationale: Facilita el drenaje venoso cerebral y reduce la presión intracraneal.

interventions.action: Programar períodos de descanso cada 15‑20 min durante la actividad
interventions.rationale: Previene la fatiga y permite recuperación neurológica.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la técnica de pacing de actividades
interventions.rationale: Promueve la autogestión y evita sobrecarga física.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de perfusión tisular cerebral ineficaz
outcomes: Presión arterial media (MAP) mantenida ≥70 mmHg durante 24 h

interventions.action: Monitorizar MAP cada hora y registrar valores
interventions.rationale: Garantiza perfusión cerebral adecuada.

interventions.action: Evaluar nivel de conciencia y pupilas cada 2 h
interventions.rationale: Detecta signos tempranos de hipoperfusión cerebral.

interventions.action: Elevar la cabecera de la cama 30° y evitar posición supina prolongada
interventions.rationale: Reduce la presión intracraneal y mejora el retorno venoso.

interventions.action: Administrar diurético osmótico (manitol) según prescripción médica
interventions.rationale: Disminuye el volumen intracraneal y la PIC.

interventions.action: Mantener hidratación adecuada, registrar ingesta y salida de líquidos
interventions.rationale: Previene hipovolemia que podría disminuir la perfusión cerebral.

interventions.action: Evitar maniobras que aumenten la presión intratorácica (toser, Valsalva)
interventions.rationale: Previene aumento secundario de la PIC.

en.summary: Excessive fluid accumulation in brain tissue that increases intracranial pressure and impairs neurological function.
key_points: Common causes: trauma, tumor, infection, heart failure, and plasma protein imbalances.
Symptoms include headache, vomiting, altered level of consciousness, and papilledema.
Diagnosis is based on CT or MRI and ICP measurement via invasive monitor.
Treatment: manage the cause, osmotic diuretics, and control ICP.

pathophysiology: Brain injury or inflammation disrupts the blood‑brain barrier.
Capillary permeability increases and interstitial fluid is retained.
Cerebral perfusion decreases due to arterial compression.
risk_factors: Infections such as meningitis or encephalitis.
signs_symptoms: Severe headache that worsens when lying down.
Vomiting without nausea or with food content.
Unequal pupils or sluggish light reaction.
diagnostics: Invasive ICP monitor: values >20 mmHg indicate intracranial hypertension.
Lab: glucose 70‑100 mg/dL, electrolytes Na⁺ 135‑145 mEq/L, K⁺ 3.5‑5.0 mEq/L.
treatment: Elevate head 30°‑45° to promote venous drainage.
Treat underlying cause (antibiotics, surgery, heart failure control).
Mechanical ventilation with positive end‑expiratory pressure (PEEP) if respiratory compromise.
complications: Cerebral ischemia from decreased blood flow.
nursing_care: Monitor vital signs and blood pressure hourly.
Assess level of consciousness using Glasgow Coma Scale.
Keep head elevated and avoid maneuvers that increase ICP.
Record urine output and fluid balance.
patient_teaching: Explain importance of keeping head elevated.
Teach recognition of worsening signs (severe headache, vomiting).
Instruct on need to adhere to treatment and imaging follow‑ups.
Encourage avoiding activities that raise intrathoracic pressure (coughing, Valsalva).

evidenced_by: changes in Glasgow scale with activity
outcomes: Activity tolerance increased to 30 min without fatigue (Borg <3)
Fatigue level ≤3 on 0‑10 scale within 48 h

interventions.action: Assess level of consciousness and Glasgow scale every 2 h
interventions.rationale: Detect early neurological decline.

interventions.action: Monitor vital signs and blood pressure hourly
interventions.rationale: Identify hemodynamic changes that may worsen ICP.

interventions.action: Maintain bed head in semi‑Fowler (30°‑45°)
interventions.rationale: Facilitates cerebral venous drainage and reduces ICP.

interventions.action: Schedule rest periods every 15‑20 min during activity
interventions.rationale: Prevents fatigue and allows neurological recovery.

interventions.action: Educate patient on pacing technique for activities
interventions.rationale: Promotes self‑management and avoids physical overload.

care_plans.diagnosis: Risk for ineffective cerebral tissue perfusion
outcomes: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) maintained ≥70 mmHg for 24 h

interventions.action: Monitor MAP hourly and record values
interventions.rationale: Ensures adequate cerebral perfusion.

interventions.action: Assess level of consciousness and pupils every 2 h
interventions.rationale: Detect early signs of cerebral hypoperfusion.

interventions.action: Elevate bed head 30° and avoid prolonged supine position
interventions.rationale: Reduces ICP and improves venous return.

interventions.action: Administer osmotic diuretic (mannitol) as prescribed
interventions.rationale: Reduces intracranial volume and ICP.

interventions.action: Maintain adequate hydration, record intake and output
interventions.rationale: Prevents hypovolemia that could lower cerebral perfusion.

interventions.action: Avoid maneuvers that increase intrathoracic pressure (coughing, Valsalva)
interventions.rationale: Prevents secondary ICP rise.

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: Any time there is an obstruction of the arteries responsible for blood flow to the brain, perfusion becomes limited, thereby causing brain cells to be deprived of vital oxygenation.

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: These patients are much more likely to have a decreased level of consciousness than patients with ischemic strokes.

sections.treatment.2.quote: It is important to understand that edema is not a discrete disorder but a sign of an underlying disorder that must be addressed.

sections.complications.1.quote: Ischemia, deprivation of oxygen, and infarction as the result of decreased perfusion cause diminished function but not always cellular death.

sections.patient_teaching.1.quote: Patients with hemorrhagic strokes will more often complain of neck pain, photosensitivity, or nausea and vomiting; patients often present with subjective complaints of the worst headache of their life.
